title: Teach2Eval: An Interaction-Driven LLMs Evaluation Method via Teaching Effectiveness
claim: Direct evaluation scores a model on static outputs; ours scores it indirectly by how much it improves weaker students through interaction.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, left direct baseline vs right multi-agent teaching loop with inset plot
description: Two dashed-border panels compare evaluation paradigms. The left panel, 'Direct Evaluation', is a vertical flow: 'data' feeds a blue Teacher LLM box, which generates a gray output box (ŷ = T(x)), and an evaluator circle 'I' with I(y = ŷ) scores it. The larger right panel, 'Teach2Eval', puts a blue Teacher LLM at top, linked by bidirectional Teach/Answer arrows to several green Student LLM boxes (LLM1, LLM2, ... LLMm). Rotated gray boxes show guidance and the students' revised answers. An evaluator circle 'I' on the right scores the students. At the far right, a red-annotated plot of Score against Turns shows an S-shaped rise with a vertical arrow marking the improvement, captioned 'The improvement of students reflects the ability of teacher.' Blue is the teacher, green the students, and red the key insight.
caption: Comparing two evaluation methods. The left shows the use of static benchmarks to directly evaluate LLMs; On the right is Teach2Eval, which generates guidance to enhance the ability of the weak model as an indirect metric for LLMs evaluation.
abstract: Recent progress in large language models (LLMs) has outpaced the development of effective evaluation methods. Evaluating LLMs with static, task-specific benchmarks is increasingly fragile due to contamination and saturation, and it fails to capture interactive reasoning. We introduce Teach2Eval, which reframes evaluation as teaching: a candidate model guides weaker students, and the students’ gains constitute the score. This interaction yields robustness to contamination and exposes orthogonal abilities with fine-grained metrics across Application, Judgment, Guidance, and Reflection. The framework scales automatically by exploiting natural error distributions from weak students, requiring neither bespoke rubrics nor human graders. Across 33 LLMs and 60 datasets, Teach2Eval achieves Spearman above 0.97 with human-preference leaderboards (e.g., Chatbot Arena/LiveBench), surpassing direct baselines, while offering actionable training signals (capability hierarchies, early overfitting) at low cost. We open-source our code and data at https://github.com/zhiqix/Teach2Eval.
